title: The medicine bag and the septic kidney
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; no doses are given. Doses come from the label, the pharmacist and the unit formulary, and the attending nephrologist decides every order.
intro:
You are the admitting internal medicine resident in the emergency room of a provincial hospital in Batangas on a Sunday night. Mrs. Teresita Manalo, 70, weighs 44 kg. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and has had fever, flank pain and vomiting for two days. The emergency team suspects pyelonephritis with sepsis.

Her creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL; it was 0.9 mg/dL six months ago. She takes metformin, bedtime insulin, losartan and hydrochlorothiazide. The intern empties her plastic bag on the table: those medicines, a strip of ibuprofen for back pain, and a bottle of “kidney cleanse” tea from a seller in the market.

n1.prompt: What do you write about her home medicines tonight?

choices.text: Continue the losartan; it protects her kidneys.
choices.feedback: When volume falls, the kidney holds filtration up with angiotensin II on the efferent arteriole. Losartan removes that lever. With a diuretic and ibuprofen on top, she has the triple combination associated with acute kidney injury (AKI), rate ratio 1.82 in the first 30 days in a large observational cohort.
choices.then: The attending, on the phone, asks you to hold the losartan, the diuretic, the metformin, the ibuprofen and the tea, and to keep her insulin with closer glucose checks.

vitals.meds: Held: losartan, diuretic, metformin, ibuprofen, tea · insulin kept

choices.text: Hold the losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, ibuprofen and tea; keep the products for identification; keep her insulin with closer glucose checks; record each decision by name.
choices.feedback: Each held item either removes a defense of filtration or accumulates when the kidney fails: metformin can contribute to lactic acidosis. The tea is a suspect until identified. Insulin stays, with more frequent checks, because stopping it invites hyperglycemia.

vitals.meds: Held: losartan, diuretic, metformin, ibuprofen, tea · insulin kept

choices.text: Hold the ibuprofen and metformin tonight; sort out the rest in the morning.
choices.feedback: A good start, but the losartan and the diuretic deepen the fall in filtration while she is dry and septic, and the tea needs to be kept and named. Decide about every product by name tonight.
choices.then: The attending asks you to hold the losartan, the diuretic and the tea too, and to keep her insulin with closer glucose checks.

vitals.meds: Held: losartan, diuretic, metformin, ibuprofen, tea · insulin kept

choices.text: Stop every medicine, insulin included, until she is eating again.
choices.feedback: Stopping insulin in a septic diabetic invites hyperglycemia. The sick-day rule keeps insulin with more frequent glucose checks and holds the medicines that harm a dry kidney.
choices.then: The nurse questions the insulin. You restart it with closer glucose checks and hold the others.

vitals.meds: Held: losartan, diuretic, metformin, ibuprofen, tea · insulin kept

n2.scene: The emergency physician has chosen an intravenous antibiotic and says, “Her creatinine is high, so I’ll give half the first dose.”

choices.text: Agree: her kidneys are failing, so a smaller dose is safer.
choices.feedback: The first dose fills the volume of distribution, the basin, and does not depend on the drain. Halving it leaves her sepsis undertreated in the hours that matter most.
choices.then: The pharmacist calls back and recommends the full first dose. It is given at 22:40.

vitals.abx: Full first dose 22:40; maintenance with pharmacist

choices.text: Hold the antibiotic until the morning creatinine shows which way it is going.
choices.feedback: A septic patient cannot wait for a creatinine. Delay risks her life, and the creatinine will not be at steady state tomorrow either.
choices.then: The attending, on the phone, asks for the full first dose now. It is given at 22:40.

vitals.abx: Full first dose 22:40; maintenance with pharmacist

choices.text: Give the full first dose now; the maintenance dose and interval get set with the pharmacist.
choices.feedback: Kidney function changes the maintenance dose, which replaces what the drains remove. It rarely changes the loading dose. Ask for the two numbers separately.

vitals.abx: Full first dose 22:40; maintenance with pharmacist

n3.scene: The laboratory has reported an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 22 mL/min/1.73 m² for tonight’s creatinine. The pharmacist asks which kidney number to use for the maintenance dose.

choices.text: None is valid tonight: her creatinine is still rising, so every equation overestimates her filtration. Dose by urine output, the clinical picture and drug levels, review daily, and write that in the chart.
choices.feedback: All the equations assume creatinine production equals excretion. In the first day of AKI the true filtration may be far lower than any equation says. As she recovers, the error reverses, so doses need daily review.

vitals.abx: Maintenance by urine output and levels; daily review

choices.text: Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance, because the label’s bands use it.
choices.feedback: Matching the label’s measure is the right habit once kidney function is stable, especially in a small older woman. Tonight her creatinine is moving, so Cockcroft–Gault is no more valid than the eGFR.
choices.then: The pharmacist points out the creatinine is still rising. You agree to dose by urine output and levels, with daily review.

vitals.abx: Maintenance by urine output and levels; daily review

choices.text: The laboratory eGFR of 22, because that is what was reported.
choices.feedback: A number on the report is not a valid number. On a rising creatinine the eGFR overestimates her filtration, and it is indexed to 1.73 m² in a 44 kg woman.
choices.then: The pharmacist questions the estimate. You agree to dose by urine output and levels, with daily review.

vitals.abx: Maintenance by urine output and levels; daily review

n4.scene: Overnight the emergency team added amikacin “for double coverage” while cultures are pending. The next dose is due at 10:00. The attending starts rounds at 09:00.
n4.prompt: What do you do about the amikacin?

choices.text: Continue it once daily with drug levels, and mention it at rounds.
choices.feedback: Once-daily dosing is the KDIGO 2012 suggestion for patients with normal kidney function in steady state (2B), which she is not. The first question is whether she needs it at all, and that needs the attending before the next dose.
choices.then: You catch the attending before 10:00. The amikacin is stopped.

vitals.abx: Amikacin stopped; single agent pending cultures

choices.text: Call the attending before the 10:00 dose: aminoglycosides should be avoided unless no suitable, less nephrotoxic alternative exists. If it is truly needed, plan it with the pharmacist and drug levels.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2012 suggests not using aminoglycosides unless no suitable, less nephrotoxic alternative is available (2A). Aminoglycosides injure the proximal tubule. A second nephrotoxin in AKI is on the module’s stop-and-call list.

vitals.abx: Amikacin stopped; single agent pending cultures

choices.text: Continue the emergency team’s order as written, in divided doses through the day.
choices.feedback: A second nephrotoxin, given in divided doses to a kidney that is still failing, is exactly what the guideline warns against. She has a less nephrotoxic option already running.
choices.then: The pharmacist flags the order and you call the attending, who stops the amikacin.

vitals.abx: Amikacin stopped; single agent pending cultures

n5.scene: She is eating, afebrile and passing normal amounts of urine. Her creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL and still falling. Her daughter asks what to do with the medicines at home.
n5.prompt: What plan do you give them?

choices.text: Never take the losartan or the metformin again; they hurt her kidneys.
choices.feedback: Losartan and metformin protect her heart, kidneys and glucose control in health. A protective drug stopped during an illness and never restarted is a harm of its own.
choices.then: The attending rewrites the plan with a sick-day card and dated restarts.

vitals.meds: Sick-day card; dated restarts; labs in 1 week

choices.text: Restart everything as before; she is better now.
choices.feedback: The ibuprofen and the tea should not come back, and her creatinine is still settling. Each restart needs a date and a check, and she needs a plan for the next time she vomits.
choices.then: The attending asks you to drop the ibuprofen and tea, date each restart, and write a sick-day card.

vitals.meds: Sick-day card; dated restarts; labs in 1 week

choices.text: A sick-day card in Tagalog with her brand names, a written restart date for losartan and metformin, no ibuprofen or tea, paracetamol at the dose the attending sets, and creatinine and potassium within a week.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2024 advises a clear plan for when held medicines restart (practice point). The card tells her what to hold when vomiting or not eating, and to restart within 24 to 48 hours of eating normally unless told otherwise.

vitals.meds: Sick-day card; dated restarts; labs in 1 week

end.title: One week later
end.text: At clinic her creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL and potassium normal. Losartan and metformin are back on their written dates, with doses rechecked against the kidney estimate each label uses now that creatinine is stable. The tea went to the hospital pharmacy for reporting. Her daughter keeps the sick-day card in the medicine box.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Decide about every product by name: the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), the renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, the diuretic, metformin and the herbal product. Keep insulin with closer checks.
  • Separate the loading dose from the maintenance dose. Kidney function changes the second, rarely the first.
  • No equation is valid while creatinine is moving. Dose by urine output, the clinical picture and drug levels, and review daily.
  • Avoid aminoglycosides unless no less nephrotoxic alternative exists (2A), and call the attending before a second nephrotoxin goes into a failing kidney.
  • Every stop needs a restart date.

See Pharmacokinetics, Which estimate, Nephrotoxins and Sick days.
